subject: China drafts export controls on its own AI models
bodyMarkdown:
If a tool you use is quietly running on a free Chinese model, Beijing spent Friday drawing the map of what it will let leave the country. The draft is open for comment until November 15, so the final shape is still being argued over.

## What Beijing put on the list

On Friday the Ministry of Commerce and the Ministry of Science and Technology published a joint draft revision to China's export control catalogue, adding 40 technologies, 23 of them in AI. The Taipei Times reported on Saturday that the AI items cover **model weights**, the trained numbers inside a model that hold everything it learned, along with source code, AI agents and computing clusters. Chip design methods are on the list too. TechNode Global reported on Sunday that comments close November 15, and that a temporary pre-export registration rule took effect the same day the draft landed, which catches deals already in progress. Reporting puts the trigger for a large model at 2 trillion parameters or more, a training run of 10^26 operations or more, or a ranking in the global top 10 on performance and safety tests. The draft itself names no model.

## The hole they left on purpose

Two carve-outs matter more than the list does. Serving a model abroad through an API, a website, an app or a SaaS platform is not counted as an export, and open-source code and published research get an exemption or a simplified licence. Deploying a restricted model into a foreign data centre is what gets caught. So Alibaba can keep answering Canadian API calls all day, while a lab that publishes its weights openly sits in an easier lane than one shipping a model abroad to run on somebody else's servers. I do not think that is sloppy drafting. China's reach in AI outside its own borders runs almost entirely on free weights anyone can download, and a rule that strangled those would hand the rest of the world straight back to American labs. The carve-outs are the policy. The list is the fence around them.

## What it changes for someone building here

Nothing in the draft is aimed at Canada. It lands here anyway, because a lot of the cheap AI running in this country is Chinese AI under somebody else's logo. If your product sits on Qwen or DeepSeek weights, you now depend on a rule written in Beijing that is not finished. Weights you already downloaded are fine, since a rule about exports cannot reach a copy that left long ago. The risk is the next release. Reporting names Moonshot's Kimi K3 and Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Max as models already past the size line, and nobody can say yet how a Chinese lab will read "globally leading" when it decides whether to open-weight its next flagship. The National reported on Friday that this arrived while the US and China trade truce was fraying.

## The takeaway

Pull down a local copy of any open model you actually depend on, because the copy in your hands is not what this rule touches. Write out today what you would switch to if your Chinese model stopped getting updates, and how many days that swap would cost you. November 15 is the date for the final text. The better signal is whether Kimi, Qwen or DeepSeek ships its next flagship with open weights, because that tells you how the labs read their own government.
